utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, could I address the Markac Defence. The Chamber would like to receive the schedule for the next two weeks, updated, especially also in view of whether the Witness Baric will testify and where we are with the translation of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Secondly, the Chamber would like to also how much time we then still needed in January, and the Chamber would also like to know whether your scheduling suggestions would include the two witnesses still pending in the motion as to be added to the witness list. And, third, the Chamber would like to know whether the Prosecution has already developed any ideas about whether or not they would like to call any rebuttal evidence. The Chamber would like to be informed about this by Monday, Tuesday. What would be -- I see already a nodding, yes, Monday. Monday, close of business. Good morning to you, Mr. Moric. Mr. Moric, I would like to remind you, as I did before, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Kay, are you ready to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm much obliged, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Moric, we had called up a document onto the screen, but we didn't deal with it, 65 ter 2D00485, and I'd like you to look at this again. This is a further report, this time from the Split-Dalmacija Police Administration, dated the 1st of September, 1995. It is a further response to a report requested by you from all the police administrations concerning crimes, as we were discussing yesterday, and we look at this period of the 22nd of August to the 31st of August, 1995. Page 2 of the English, please. Mr. Cipci, who has signed this report, then goes through the various issues in response to your request, giving you details. In paragraph 3, we can see he has dealt with an issue of arson, and then removal of mainly deserted movable property, and reports against 24 persons for 10 crimes. Just looking at that issue in paragraph 3, giving a police perspective, how easy is it for the police to control and protect people's homes if the people have moved out of the those homes? Is there a weakening of the possibility to protect because there's no one there within the property?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, it is commonly known in the police practice that a thief will always seize an opportunity where there is one. Theft will occur where two conditions are met: that there is something to be stolen and that there's an opportunity to do so. Had the inhabitants occupied their homes at the time, the incidents of crimes would have been much lower, not only within the territory covered by this particular police administration, but in all the other ones as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So when comparisons are drawn between normal times, before an area has been the subject of conflict, and then abnormal times, would it be right to say that the comparisons have to be carefully looked into before drawing conclusions as to the number of police there may be needed in normal times as against the police that were here at this time?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, this is something that needs to be factored in as part of preparations, and assessment has to be made of possible developments and expectations. Under normal circumstances, when citizens occupy their homes and when there is normalcy to life, guarding citizens, and that's to say their lives and their property, in an inhabited area requires normally one police patrol cruising the area and reacting where necessary. However, under the circumstances prevailing at the time, it was almost necessary for every house to be guarded by one policeman. That's the difference between work in normal conditions and work in the context we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in your planning, had you realised or the Ministry of Interior realised that people would be deserting homes, so that private property would be left unguarded and more of a target for thieves and criminals?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of our planning, we did envisage that a certain number of citizens from the area would leave for various reasons. Unfortunately, this is the usual course of events in wartime circumstances. However, we did not think that the numbers would be that high. There was no rational reason, from our point of view, for this to happen en masse. Besides, when we were preparing our tasks in the area, we felt that the appeal issued by the president of our state and the prime minister, which had been repeatedly broadcast over the media and which called upon the local citizens to stay, we felt that that was very relevant. Therefore, there was no reason why we should have predicted that as many people would leave as did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we just look at this passage in paragraph 3 at the end, where Mr. Cipci states: "According to information gathered so far, none of the liberated areas stand out as particularly affected by the aforementioned crimes, and the perpetrators are for the most part from these areas or from the immediate vicinity." Did that sentence convey any particular meaning to you? What did you conclude from that, when that information was given to you?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the Police Administration reports herein that the perpetrators were persons hailing from the area or from the immediate surroundings. This should indicate, and this was proved right by the subsequent developments, that these were isolated crimes which evidently occurred, and unfortunately so, from base instincts such as gain or revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Looking at Mr. Cipci's report in paragraph 4: "Except in the case of fire, where civilian personnel carried out an on-site investigation alone, these were not performed in other cases since the cases concerned the removal of items from an open and unprotected area, where there were no characteristic traces as a result of the acts themselves." So there Mr. Cipci appears to be given a reason for not performing on-site investigations in certain cases. Could you comment on that as to whether that was right or wrong in the context of the time?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not at all wrong, in view of the police practice. If we have the crime of theft, of misappropriation of property of another, the owner, however, not being present at the scene of the crime and not being able to help the criminal investigation in any way, and where no trace evidence is left at the crime scene which would allow to identify perpetrators, and where there are no eye-witnesses who might help with the identification, in other words, if there is nothing left to do but to make note of the fact that the property of another went missing, then, as is customary in policing work, it is necessary to wait for a period of time until the owner of the stolen property reports the crime and provides the necessary information for the identification of the property stolen and possibly identify potential perpetrators. In other words, Mr. Cipci reported here that, for instance, there had been cases where there was reason to suspect that livestock had been stolen from estates and nearby fields, but there is little in the way of traces that one can find in such cases of theft. This, however, does not mean at all that the police would desist from attempts to solve such cases of crime as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We've no need to look at 5. If we look at point 6, and the report here from Mr. Cipci, next page in the English, please - thank you: "Appropriate criminal investigations are planned and underway into all the recorded crimes." What did you understand that part of the report to mean?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, the key word in this sentence is "recorded." It is being reported that the police is engaged in a criminal investigation into all the crimes that it was put on notice of; in other words, of all the crimes that it is aware of having happened. "Crimes recorded" means that the police are aware of the crimes based on all the sources which it can possibly rely on in elucidating crimes, be it an eye-witness who reported it, be it the injured party who reported it, or be it the police, themselves, through witnessing it on the ground, or be it some of the representatives of international organisations or personnel of other state and local services who may have reported the crime. The fact that the crime was recorded refers to all the crimes that the police had been put on notice of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning now to paragraph 7. We know from paragraph 3 that reports were received against 24 persons for 10 crimes, and we see in paragraph 7 five perpetrators known wearing Croatian Army uniforms during the commission of the crimes in relation to which the VP was informed. Now, that figure of 5 perpetrators out of 24 persons concerning 10 crimes, what were you able to conclude from that figure?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless I'm mistaken, and I can't see the beginning of the document, I think the document was sent on the 1st of September. Is it possible, perhaps, to see the beginning of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is the 1st of September, yes.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of that, it can be concluded that unfortunately individuals wearing military uniforms are still found to be perpetrating crimes, on the one hand. On the other hand, this particular formulation leads to conclude that the military police were informed, just as the sentence goes on to say that they are in the process of identifying them, which is an initial stage in the criminal inquiry. They are to identify the potential perpetrators and then commence a criminal investigation. A more precise answer to your question would be that it can be concluded that by that time, unfortunately, there was still perpetrators to be found wearing military uniforms. However, evidently co-operation with the military police improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's that issue of wearing the military uniform that I want to look at more specifically. The fact that someone was in a military uniform at this time did not prove that that person was in the military at that time; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, it does not prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think this question has been put to 50 witnesses 70 times. If it's an introduction, then I think that is a matter which is so obvious in this case that the one is not a proof of the other, that it was a superfluous question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour headed me off too early. It was, in fact, a stand-alone question because this formulation of words is being sent to Mr. Moric, which is why I wanted to put it to him, so that we had him dealing with it without being controversial to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wouldn't expect anyone to say, Well, of course, that's perfect proof, someone wearing a uniform, he must be at least a colonel in the army. That's something that -- but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the Court's comment. Thank you very much. May this document be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1857.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And there are two more of these documents I want to go through with you, Mr. Moric, in the interests of time, to make them exhibits of the Court. Can we have 2D00354.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a similar report in relation to your earlier instructions, documents we have seen in evidence, of the 22nd of August, 30th of August, requiring reports from your police administrations. This one is from Glina Police Administration, implementation of measures. You can see that the information follows what we have seen before. Can we go to page 2 of the English, please. We see there that this particular police administration has broken it down into the police stations within the Police Administration, and giving particular details there. May we go to page 3 of the English and looking at number -- the next page in the Croatian. We see further details there, as well as details of on-site investigations. If the English can be turned over, please. We can see the types of crimes; burnings, one explosion, other details. If we may turn over and go to paragraph 6, please. On this page here, we see as well identification of perpetrators. We see it broken down as to how it is expressed in this document in paragraph 7, that there is the specific identifying factor of people being members of the HV and how that is expressed. Again, this follows the previous pattern of reports to you; is that correct, Mr. Moric? I don't need to go into any further detail.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It follows the previous pattern, and as I said, specific details were needed so that I could take any decisions on management on the basis of specific data and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. May this document be made an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D1858.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document is 2D00166. A further report, 2nd of September, from the Lika-Senj Police Administration in Gospic, sent by Mr. Dasovic, the police administration chief, to you, in response to your request for reports, of the 30th of August, giving us details that we can see. If we turn to page 2 in the English, we can see the breakdown of information, including, in paragraph 3, perpetrators of crimes from Gospic Police Station turn out to be mainly members of the HV, but cases where civilians involved, giving details of the investigations in paragraph 5. If we go to the last page in the English to paragraph 7, on the same page in the Croatian, 14 civilians, 8 members of the Croatian Army, were recorded as perpetrators. Again, a similar report to that which we've seen before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But if you allow me, I wish to point out a formulation in item 3 which I find to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could go back to paragraph 3, which is the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Continue giving your evidence.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under item 3, the chief of the Police Administration says that cases of burning of houses and removal of movable property still occur, but to a lesser degree. So this is relevant for managing the activities. This still occurs, but to a lesser degree. So a gradual decrease of the occurrence of these crimes is something that is noted here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1859.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1859 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to the next document, the last in this series, 2D00087. This is a report by Mr. Dasovic again on the 12th of September, but in response to your original request for reports of all the police administrations on the 22nd of August, and so it covers the period from the 22nd of August until the 10th of September, as we see in paragraph 5 when we get to it. If you could just look at paragraph 1, and now if we could turn over the English, it gives the same information that we have seen before. Military police are not sufficiently present, military police not paying enough attention to the problems. When acting on their own, military police do not investigate perpetrators thoroughly, which impedes the uncovering of crimes, resulting in a number of them remaining unsolved. Is there any comment you can make as to whether there is a disparity between the professional competence of the military police officers as compared with those officers from the Ministry of Interior, the civilian police officers?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately there was disparity at the time. As I already mentioned during my testimony, while establishing the state, its mechanisms also needed to be set up. So as the military was being formed, so along the way the military police needed to be formed as well. The civilian police supported this process of setting up military police by expert training and by educating the management and the command structures of military police. At this time, the military police, as an institution, was two or two and a half years old, so it is clear that there was a disparity, but the difference in the professional level and competence is one issue and one problem; and another issue, another problem, is the difference in terms of the level of organisation and readiness for rapid reaction. It is obvious that at that time the military police infrastructure was not good enough so as to be able to follow civilian police in their activities, but we also had a legal issue there because the military police was supposed to discharge duties from its area of responsibility, and that was why we constantly insisted on this co-operation. So the military police certainly had difficulties and problems. We also had great problems within the civilian police, for sure, but we had to co-operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The Court can see the rest of the document. If we just turn quickly to page 3 in the English, page 2 in the Croatian, to note 33 on-site investigations for the types of crimes ranging from burning of houses, mining of housing facilities, illegal possession of weapons, ammunition, explosive devices, 66 perpetrators, 57 civilians, 9 HV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1860.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1860 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For the final part of my questioning of you, Mr. Moric, I want to turn now to the issue concerning any restrictions of movement there may have been imposed upon people. If we could first turn to the document Exhibit D28, and this is a document dated the 6th of August, 1995, and it concerns an agreement between the state of Croatia and the UNCRO forces for Sector North and Sector South. This document was signed by Mr. Sarinic and Mr. Akashi. Firstly, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember this specific document at present, but I could say with certainty that I must have been aware of it. But at the moment, I cannot remember whether I ever had it before me. However, I'm almost certain that I had to have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because you were in the position of being in charge of the fundamental civilian police, this agreement between UNCRO and Mr. Sarinic, what would that have represented to you in terms of legal status of the document?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to read the document now. But -- so that we wouldn't lose time, I think that nothing could be agreed by this document that was not already a part of the national legislation. I believe that the Secretary-General's envoy, Mr. Akashi, was potentially concerned about the freedom of movement and the security of the mission's personnel, and that the purpose of this document was probably to emphasise, on the one hand, from the international perspective, the obligation to protect human rights and freedoms of all citizens in the Republic of Croatia, and, on the other hand, to reach an agreement about not restricting the movements of the personnel of the international mission of UN, and guaranteeing support for their security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm interested in the transmission of this document. From its date of the 6th of August, are you able to say if you received a copy of this document on that date or any later date, as a document for you to study and take into account?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, in my answer to your previous question, I said that I could not say with any certainty whether I had this document before me and whether I had seen it previously, but I suppose that I ought to have been aware of it. I have heard about it, so I cannot exclude the possibility that I received it. But also I cannot exclude the possibility that I did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why I ask this question is for this reason: This Court has heard from various international witnesses, from UNCRO or the European Monitoring Mission and others, about cases of civilian police officers obstructing the passage or preventing the passage of internationals from those organisations at various check-points. And, firstly, were you aware of cases where that happened?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is relevant to say at the beginning that such instructions to restrict the movements of the personnel of any of the international missions or organisations is something that I never issued. If it did occasionally happen on the ground, I do not remember that I received any specific reports on that or, more precisely, that I received such reports and that I did not react. It is true that I'm talking about a period when there were so many events that it is possible I do not remember any such reports, but I am certain that if I was informed about such incidents, that I would have reacted in the sense of issuing instructions that they have to be allowed freedom of movement. And if there were any sporadic incidences of vehicles being stopped and the personnel controlled, then it could have happened due to the specific circumstances in the area, such as, for example, once or twice vehicles with marks of international organisations, such as UNPROFOR and UNCRO, and later on UNHCR, were stolen, and it is possible that upon receiving their local tasks, that is to say, to search for this equipment and the people who had stolen it, the regular police could have stopped such vehicles and tried to check who was in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, could we try to keep the witness talking about facts. Of course, it's possible, nothing can be excluded, that if a UN car is stolen, that you start investigating it by stopping UN cars. Do you have any knowledge of what happened, because your answer suggests that the only purpose for which you are aware of for which vehicles from international organisations were stopped would have been to search for stolen vehicles? Is that how we have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the police did not have any other valid reasons. That is how I would state that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether they had valid reasons to do so. My question was whether that was the case, yes or not, with or without valid reasons. Could you tell us what you know about this, even from reports? But knowledge about facts; not about what should have been, but about what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. Yes, that was the reason for them to be stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it to say that whenever a vehicle of an international organisation was stopped, that that would have been the only reason for doing so, never for any other reason? If you don't know, tell us. If you do know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know that, and I said so in one of my previous answers. The reason was their own security and also a search for stolen vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've told us that you didn't go through the document you said you must have been aware of at the time. Who decides on whether or not the security of members of the international organisations is at stake? Is it they, themselves, who decide whether or not to freely move around, with all the risks, or is it the Croatian government who is entitled to say, Stop, it's too dangerous for you? If I say "Croatian government," I mean Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in principle, yes, but this is not what I had in mind. I had in mind the specific developments in local areas because of which the police would have to stop anyone, including the peacekeeping mission's personnel or personnel of international organisations, until the reason for stopping them did not exist anymore. But, generally speaking, the Croatian government was in the position to say, Yes, you can move freely in certain areas, or, You cannot go into specific areas until such and such a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the master of the freedom of movement was finally the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you told us that you had not looked at the document, the agreement. Is there any -- would there be anything in the agreement you said you did not re-read, but as you told us you were aware of at the time, which would confirm that or contradict that, or was there any clause in that agreement which would be relevant for the answers to the last questions I put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry that I cannot say with any certainty whether I did receive this document or not. Only if I were to read all of it, then I could answer with more certainty to your very precise question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not inviting you to do so at this very moment. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In looking at the documents in this case, Mr. Moric, we've seen a large number of orders. We've been through quite a few, you and I, in the last day. The Court has even more. We haven't seen an order from you to the police administrations setting out the Akashi-Sarinic agreement so that the police administrations were aware of it. Do you know if you drafted any such order at the time? We haven't got one in this case.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember doing anything in relation to one such document, though I do understand the idea behind the document, as I explained in my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm interested in what happened at the time, which is why I asked whether this document had ever been transmitted to you, because again I found no evidence anywhere of anyone sending it to you. And you're a person dealing with freedom of movement at the time, and that is why I asked whether the document was transmitted to you at that time. So I'm very concerned to know what was sent to you at the time, what you knew at the time, and what you did at the time, because there is this issue of the civilian police being recorded as having stopped various international representatives. Do you understand? Are you able to give any further information concerning the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I can only repeat that I'm sorry that I don't remember having been given the document or hearing of it. I do understand the point it makes and why it was written. As for the freedom of movement of personnel of international organisations is concerned, I understand that it could have been restricted to a locality for a limited period of time, such as an area or a brief dangerous operation close to a roadway, and other reasons that would deal with the security of international personnel in general of all the various missions, de-mining operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, your question was answered at page - what is it? - 17 or 18, line 23. Could you make sure that the witness refrains from telling us what could have been the case, or what he could imagine that would have been the case, not having looked at documents, so as to leave the realm of speculation, unless there is a very good basis for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is, actually, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the next question. Can we go to Exhibit D499.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's a document dated the 17th of August, 1995, and in fact it does concern UNCRO, UNCIVPOL, European Union Monitors. It was written by you. I'd like you to look at it. You sent it to all the police administrations. Page 2 in the English, please. It doesn't refer to the Akashi-Sarinic agreement or any agreement between the Croatian government and the UN, which is why I'm interested about who received this agreement, where it went to, who knew about it, what the efficiency of the system was, whatever. But we see here, on the 17th of August, that you issued this order to the police administrations concerning no longer to need restriction of movement in areas because of the return and normalisation of life, and consequently do not restrict the movement of European Union Monitors, UNCIVPOL, UNCRO members, "movements and itineraries of UNHCR convoys must be announced in advance." Now, just before we look at that document, was there any plan or policy from the Ministry of Interior that had been issued or sent to the civilian police on the ground saying, Restrict the movement of internationals, prevent them from going to places? Was there a plan or policy in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: There absolutely was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the reason, on the 17th of August, of you sending this to all the police administrations concerning the international monitors, can you recollect why you put that in this document on the 17th of August?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the preamble, the document refers to the general state of security which allows for free movement of persons and goods, as well as a gradual normalisation of life. In other words, there is no need to restrict the freedom of movement for security reasons. This was to state that if anyone was still in doubt, there was no need to restrict the movement of members of international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I want you now to look at a document dated the 8th of August, Exhibit D1769, please. This was an order issued by you again to all the police administrations. Its subject is the arrival of reporters and public figures in the liberated areas. We can see in paragraph 1 it refers to accredited reporters. We can see, in paragraph 2, about: "... distinguished and generally-known public persons entering the liberated area, consult the duty operations of the Ministry of Interior operation return staff, and for all other persons access to the liberated area is prohibited until further notice." If you could inform the Court about the purpose of this order issued on the 8th of August, please, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, always in all my documents, since I'm in charge of prevention, the purpose of all my documents is security and safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can now go to the Akashi-Sarinic agreement, as I would like you to look at it to see its context, what it says, and then I'll ask questions about it to you. So can we have Exhibit D28, please. Please have a look at this, Mr. Moric. An agreement between the Government of the Republic of Croatia, the United Nations peace forces, temporary measures in the areas formerly known as Sector South. If you could just read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you were referring to the title of the document only, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, sorry, the whole document. It concerns the effects of hostilities on the lives of civilians. It's committed to minimising loss of civilian life from hostilities, full protection of civilians and human rights, humanitarian needs.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. May we move further down, because in Croatian I can only see item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps if we turn to page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page in Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you finished it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. First of all, would this agreement, signed by Mr. Sarinic with Mr. Akashi, have been relevant to the business of the Ministry of Interior, to the work of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been relevant, in the context of items 4 and 5, if I've read them correctly, where security reasons are cited, and in relation to them, the issues of movement and security guarantees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If this had been transmitted to you at the time --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question. The witness has reiterated that he cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first hear what the question is. At the same time, Mr. Kay is put on notice that speculating on hypothetical situations is not what at least the Prosecution expects him to invite the witness to do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it's not speculation, Your Honour, because I asked for any evidence that there may be that the Prosecution has that this was transmitted at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not say that you were asking for speculation. I said that you were on notice that you would not ask for speculation. And, therefore, not having heard your question, I have no opinion about whether you would or would not ask for speculation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, if you had received this document at the time, would you have issued an order to all your police administrations, telling them about their rights and obligations under it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, of course what Mr. Kay is asking, of course, he's asking a hypothetical situation. If he rephrases his question slightly, then the question remains the same and your objections would not be valid anymore. That is, If you would have seen this at the time, was it or had it been your duty... And then he tells about what his duties are, and that comes down to exactly the same. So let's refrain from semantic discussions. At the same time, Mr. Kay, you're asking what he would have done under different situation, whereas I do understand you wanted to ask him what he felt his duty would have been to do, which is slightly different but comes down to the same considerations when answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, if you had received this document, would you have had any duty or responsibility to take any action upon it in relation to the police administrations beneath you?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, in my previous answer I said that I thought the document was relevant in items 4 and 5, which came within the competence of the Ministry of the Interior. I believe that under the circumstances, I would have drafted instructions which I would have sent to police administrations in order to let them know of the existence of the document and of the obligations they had arising from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because I note that when we looked at Exhibit D499, there is no mention there of the agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the United Nations peace forces, is that any indication to you as to what information you had at that time between the 6th of August and 17th of August? Are you able to give a comment on that, the absence of reference to this agreement in any of those orders?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have happened this way only because I evidently was not aware of the document and did not have any obligations with regard to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to now consider the process, because we have here, on the one hand, an agreement signed by Mr. Akashi, on behalf of the United Nations peacekeeping forces, and we have Mr. Sarinic, who had a particular job, signing on behalf of the Republic of Croatia. What should have been -- or was there any legal route that needed to be taken for this to be acted upon by you at that time?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my experience dating from that time, and from the standard practice, I can tell you which route it should have taken. Mr. Sarinic was the head of office of the President of the Republic. He should have sent it to the Government of the Republic of Croatia, a member of which was the minister of the interior. The government could have set out some of its positions with regard to how the agreement would be implemented. The positions thus set out would be taken on board by the minister of the interior, who would, in turn, inform one of his assistants about it and give his obligations about it, the one assistant who was charged with it, and that would have been me. So that would have been the proper route.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to comment upon it, its status in law, then, as it is just signed by Mr. Akashi and Mr. Sarinic? What was its legal status, this agreement between Mr. Akashi and Mr. Sarinic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this question. I don't know what the foundation for this question is, whether this witness is in any position to express an opinion of the legality of an agreement of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, in view of the position of this witness at the time and the fact that he may have had to consider the legal validity of this document, it is certainly interesting to know not what a legal status of this agreement was, as Mr. Kay asked him, but how he understands such a document, in view of its legal validity. Then it is about his own relevant opinion he may have formed on it. At the same time, Mr. Kay, we've heard from this witness first that -- with certainty, that he was aware of the document. Two pages later, he certainly was -- he apparently was not aware of the document. So let's try to keep it short. He says he may have seen the document, but he cannot say with certainty that he has seen the document. So in order to explore his understanding of this document, which he may have seen, may not have seen, certainly may not have seen, certainly may have seen, is a risky exercise, but let's ask, now that he has read it, whether he remembers whether at the time he formed an opinion about any agreement, for example this one, being concluded between Mr. Sarinic and Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I've dealt with the issue of whether he had seen it at the time, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have dealt with it. I'm just noting that there are some -- the answers are not in every respect consistent. I don't want to revisit that whole matter, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which is why I took him to the other exhibits, and the content of those exhibits and what is written in them. We're now very familiar with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then he concludes from the documents that he has not seen it. That is a conclusion, and if three minutes before that, without having seen the documents, he has a different recollection, then at least it's something the Chamber will have to consider, what the basis is for the testimony of the witness in this respect. Not to say that it's one or the other, but certainly a matter to pay proper attention to. As I said before, it may be relevant to know whether the witness formed any opinion about this kind -- the validity of this kind of agreement, because that is apparently what you are looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Give me just a straight single answer. This agreement we've been looking at, at that time between the 6th and 17th of August, can you say that you saw this document and acted upon it by informing your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question. I think the witness has answered this question twice, and I could take --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd be happy with the answers, but there seems to be uncertainty about it. But if I'm the only one who's happy with the answers, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, answers, Mr. Kay. The Chamber will consider -- the evaluation of the evidence, of course, is for the Chamber to -- but I just pointed at the various questions and the various answers we received in relation to having seen at the time the document, yes or no. I'm not going any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am surprised the Prosecution objects. I mean, a large portion of their case is based on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but whether you're surprised or not on what Ms. Mahindaratne does, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, we were searching --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm on my last minute, Mr. Moric. In your position, as assistant minister of interior for the fundamental police, we have seen you have issued orders to your subordinate police administrations concerning freedom of movement. In fact, the Court has seen other documents on the same matter from you, and we have also seen comments on documents from you. This document, signed by Mr. Sarinic, could you have acted upon it if it had just been given to you by Mr. Sarinic, or would it have had to have gone through another procedure for you to have issued lawful orders in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, in answer to your earlier question, I described the procedure that was in place in the time and that this should have gone through in order to reach the government and, consequently, the minister, and then the assistant minister ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I'd like to ask you a few questions from your statements and maybe further questions based on the questions asked by my colleagues Mr. Mikulicic and Mr. Kay. I'll do my best not to repeat those matters, but if I happen to jump between subjects, it's just that I'm trying to use the time as efficiently as possible. So bear with me if you can; okay?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, during the examination by my learned friend Mr. Mikulicic, he discussed with you the operation return plans, and we don't need to bring that up, but it is embodied in your document D1845. And in that plan, Mr. Moric, you had envisioned working with the UN as part of the peaceful integration, and it was also contemplated that the people who resided there were going to continue to reside there while this peaceful reintegration was taking place; is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They were the citizens of the Republic of Croatia, and it was envisaged that they would continue to reside there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, of course, we know, based on the facts of this case and what transpired, that things became much different than this morning. You were asked some questions by Mr. Kay, and for reference, Mr. President and Your Honours, it's page 3 and 4 of today's transcript, concerning the Serbs leaving the area, and while you expected some Serbs to leave, you didn't expect as many to leave. And my question, I would like to ask you -- I want to expand on a few items touched upon by Mr. Kay and talk about -- in addition to the looting issues that you talked about, can you talk on all levels how your policing job became more difficult when there were no people left in the area? I don't want you to just limit it to just looting. How, in toto, did it become more difficult? And, likewise, could you include as part of that, did it become more dangerous for your police officers?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, it was much more difficult to do the police work in such an area because of the fact that, as I have already mentioned, in the wake of Operation Storm a time of confusion followed, as is typical for such periods, that is to say, a postwar period. The policemen discharged their duties in a complex security situation which brought them in danger as well, because a group of paramilitary and para-police had remained in the area and because there were a lot of mines and other explosives devices and weapons left behind in this area, as well as because of the fact that houses and private property had been abandoned in such great numbers, and also because from the neighbouring Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the parts that were under the control of Republika Srpska, groups returned to the area liberated in Operation Storm with some specific goals, and also because of the fact that this was a vast area. We talked about how big it was yesterday. And these are all the elements that show how difficult were the conditions under which the police work was supposed to be done, and the scope of duties was increasing from day to day so that around the 15th of August, we were faced with a spate of negative events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if I was to ask you the precise question, did the fact that there were very few people left in the area make your job more or less difficult?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if I would repeat what the witness said earlier is that he said that since people were not there, that reporting took place rather late. Apart from that it's obvious that if there's no one there, it may be very difficult to observe that a crime is committed, apart from those who commit the crimes. And of course you wouldn't expect any reports to the police in that respect. That is what the witness explained at quite some length. If there's anything else you would seek in your answer -- and I'm making this observation because the previous question resulted in an answer which was, for 85 per cent, a repetition of what the witness said already before; confusion, large territory. The only thing that was new, I think, was the groups that returned from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Republika Srpska. So, therefore, if you're seeking anything apart from what is either obvious or already in the testimony of the witness, I would invite you to focus on those specific matters and not after lengthy introductions, but let's go to the core right away. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I appreciate Your Honour's guidance. My specific question, just so Your Honour knows, and I'll move on to another topic, was that during the examination of Mr. Kardum, the Prosecution took a different position. But I will focus my questions based on Your Honour's guidance, but I just wanted to bring that to Your Honour's attention so you had an idea of why I was going into that in a little more depth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As may appear from my observation, I carefully listened to the testimony of the witness, which covered 90 per cent again of what you asked him. So let's try to find that final 10 per cent immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moric, yesterday in your testimony you talked about the number of police officers that you would have needed to secure the area, and at page 25647, lines 16 and 17, you said that not even 40.000 men would have been enough. And there were serious problems for the fundamental police in manning check-points, and I'm talking about manpower concerns and their ability to prevent people coming into the area, were there not?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Counsel. And in addition to that, we did not have a legal valid basis to prevent freedom of movement, except in exceptional micro-local situations and locations. So the answer to your question is, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk -- and I would like to go through a sequence of the problems facing the military police. And let's just, for a starting point, go into some check-points, to a degree, and some of the difficulties that the police were facing. And I would like to bring up 65 ter 1D3013. Now, Mr. Moric, I don't suspect that you've seen this document before, but I trust that you recognise the format of this document, given your many years in the Police Department in the Ministry of the Interior. And as you can see, this is a 9 August 1995 report from the Benkovac Police Station. And if we could move to page 2 in the English, and stop me if you you need more time to examine the document. Now, if we look at -- this is a report from 1400 hours to 2200 hours on the 9th of August, and I'm interested in the first paragraph on the reporting that came in: "After being informed of new events in the police station, Cunjak, Zivko, Pecirovic, Midhat, patrolled all the check-points in the town several times, as well as the officers on patrol, at which point there was no particular new events aside from the fact that the officers at the Smilcic check-point informed us that civilian persons dressed in military uniforms were coming to the village Biljane Donje and burning houses. The same were arriving to the village on traffic and side roads." Now, obviously this document indicates that the MUP was receiving reports of civilians in military uniforms conducting burnings as early as the 9th of August. My question for you, Mr. Moric, is: Reports back concerning the effectiveness of check-points and the difficulty in those check-points, given the fact that people, who may have known the area, knew the side roads, did that present a difficulty for your men?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report, police officers precisely point out that people are using traffic and side roads to get to certain points, and of course this presented a great difficulty because of the great number of such roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And obviously all these side roads couldn't be patrolled continuously by the civilian police, could they?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an operative and technical request at the level of commanders of police stations, and I believe that whenever they could meet the request, they did do so. But generally speaking, it's certain there were more side roads and traffic roads than they had police patrols at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I ask you that question because several witnesses for the Prosecution have come forward to say that the only thing that the civilian police had to do to prevent people that were interested in committing crimes is to just put up more check-points and make sure these people weren't coming into the area. What's your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that is not correct. If that was the mechanism that would have prevented such development, we would have used it. But even if these traffic roads and side roads were blocked, the perpetrators who were from the area were well-acquainted with the area, and they moved around it in various ways mostly on foot in order to avoid any police check-points or control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we will offer into evidence 1D3013.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1861.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1861 is admitted into evidence. If you would allow me, Mr. Kehoe, to seek a bit of clarification on this same report which is still on the screen. Mr. Moric, the first paragraph about persons coming to the village and using traffic and side roads, if I read that, I get the impression, but please correct me or at least give me your impression, that apparently these people going to the village were escaping the check-points and, therefore, not checked before they went to such a village, that is what I'm inclined to understand what is reported here. Do you agree with that, or do you have a different understanding of what is said in this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is also how I understand it. That was a way to avoid police check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I also read this document as reporting that for these reasons, they could not be arrested or that they escaped further action from police officers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, and that is precisely the conclusion that can be drawn from this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if we read it this way, do you have an explanation how, under those circumstances, you could establish, first of all, that persons were dressed in military uniforms, but if you could already observe that perhaps from a distance, how you could establish that these were civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a report drafted by police officers, and they are reporting to the commander of the police station that through their colleagues, that is to say, someone who is a member of the Ministry of the Interior and discharging some duties within the MUP, informed them of the arrival of persons dressed in military uniforms. So this is local knowledge and local familiarity with certain persons. This is how I understand it. And I conclude that those who had seen these men recognised that these citizens were dressed in military uniforms, but they knew that these same persons were not soldiers and were not from the ranks of the Croatian Army. This is how I would interpret this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, it is your understanding this must have been based on observations by persons from this village, Biljane Donje, and that they would have recognised those persons as being civilians and, at the same time, being dressed in military uniforms, in which case I would expect - but please correct me when I'm wrong - that a police officer would report those details, saying, I recognise Mr. X, Y, or Z, whom I know to be a civilian, although he was dressed in a military uniform, of which we do not find further details in this report. Is that also -- is that what you would expect as well, as an experienced police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, your conclusion is correct because the report contains certain indications that would incite the crime police to collect the facts, and they would very quickly establish who these citizens were, because it is clear from this formulation that the people who had seen them had also recognised them as citizens dressed in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you started thinking in terms of assumptions, that is, I assume that they had been informed about this and this and this. And now in this step of your answer you say it's easy to define them because they had been observed. So you make -- what you earlier assumed to be the basis for these findings, you now make them facts. I'm not yet at that point, without further verification. But you would say if that is what happened and if this knowledge was brought to the attention of the crime police, then that would have created a situation in which it may have been relatively easy to identify the perpetrators. I think, then, if that is how I can understand your answer, then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go back to the first page of this document, I'd like to ask you some clarifying questions based on the questions asked by the Presiding Judge. Now, this is a work order, is it not, that the individual shift presents, and he presents this back to his supervisor for additional steps to be made based on this information; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I wish to correct your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not a shift. It is not a shift, because there are several police patrols in one shift and more policemen. This is just one patrol, and there's a number of these within one shift. This is a work order with listed tasks that they need to carry out, and previously we saw their report that in connection with the tasks that were issued to them, they carried out certain activities, including the information they gathered. After that, this is forwarded to other services within the police station, and from that report each of these services can see what is relevant for it and what it needs to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just to follow up on that, you mentioned the crime police. If information like this is passed to this police officer's superior, it could be sent to the crime police for further investigation; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In case of this fact, when the policemen entered something specific that they learned in their report, I do not agree that they could pass it on to the crime police. They would have to pass it on to the crime police within the police station to conduct further investigation about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when we look at this work order and these comments, if this is going to continue to be investigated, this matter -- this information is not the end of the investigation; it could be the beginning of the investigation that leads to the crime police conducting interviews or doing anything that they have to do to investigate the matter?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. This is just the initiation of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me shift to some of the other difficulties facing the civilian police, and you alluded to several of them this morning, and one of them that you alluded to was the issue of being confronted with ammunition and mines in the liberated areas. And I'd like to show you a serious of documents and ask you if this is the type of information that you had in mind. And I'll go through several of them in sequence and then just ask you for your assessment of them at the end. And I do that in the spirit of time, because some of them are similar, they're just in different places at different times. If we could go to the first document, which is 1D3018. And just so you know, Mr. Moric, while this is coming up, they're all virtually two-page documents, so we'll go through the two pages. And when you tell me you're completed reviewing them, we can go to the next one. Now, this is a work order for the 6th Benkovac Police Station for the 13th of August.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will say, Mr. President, I do believe this is mis-dated, because it's 1994. I think contextually, it would appear to be 1995. If we can look at the next page, and focusing most of our attention on paragraphs 4, 5, and 6, which deals with the issue of ammunition and mines. Have you completed reviewing it? Let's look at another one which is 1D --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I think I was getting French there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm getting the French on Channel 4. I know the language myself, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't notice it. I'm used to listening to several languages. Usually, if it's observed, it's immediately repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn, Mr. Moric, to 1D3020, another work order from the Benkovac Police Station, 14-15 August 1995. Again, if you view the first page, I think it's self-explanatory. In the English, if we can turn to the second page, I believe we can -- it goes two pages in B/C/S, yes. And we're interested in the bottom paragraph, concerning the finding of explosives. And, again, just let me know when you're finished reading that.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn to another one, 1D3021, another 14-15 August document. Excuse me, I apologise, not that document. If I can turn to 1D3023. My apologies. And this is dated 16 August.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page in this document, please. This is -- the pertinent paragraphs being paragraph 1 and 3 for the purposes of my question.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moric, I'm just using these three as an example, and all three of them talk about the finding of plastic explosives, weapons, ammunition, explosives, et cetera, in houses throughout the liberated area. Were these the type of reports that you were receiving back from people in the field that they were finding throughout the liberated area once the police were moving through?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't receive this sort of reports, but I did receive reports through my daily contacts with chiefs of police administrations which made it quite clear that they, having received such reports from the field, were aware of the problem. And it was clear that the problem required special involvement on the part of the police because the ammunition, which ranged from regular ammunition to anti-aircraft rockets, had to be safely evacuated from the area, and this undoubtedly required special engagement on the part of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we'll offer into evidence 1D3018, 1D3020, and 1D3023.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, those documents become Exhibit D1862 up to D1864, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. One second. D1862 up to and including D1864 are admitted into evidence. Could I ask one question in relation to the last documents we saw. Was there a general duty to report to the police for every citizen in that area? And if so, where is that duty to be found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is my understanding correct that you asked me if the citizens were duty-bound to report that they were in possession of such weapons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not in possession of weapons, but just ordinary citizens. We find in this report that three elderly people were found, and people of 60 years and over, among them a woman of 65 years old, and apparently there's an issue of whether they had already reported to the Benkovac Police Station. Therefore, I ask you whether there was any duty and whether it was -- what was the reason to verify whether they had report it already. I do not see in this report that they were in any way related to any weapons, but if I misread, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did not misread it, Your Honour. They were not tied in with the weapons. That's not the point. The point is that they had the duty to report because the duty stems from the law governing residence of citizens. Following the liberation of the area, the legal system of the Republic of Croatia was restored to the area. And under the legislation of the time the citizens were still not in possession of what were the legal identity documents, so they were still duty-bound to report their residence if they stayed in the area before the conflict and renewed their documents, because what they had previously were para-documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even those who were born in that same village would not have had any of their original documents dating from, well, before 1991? Because it appears that all three were born in that same village where they were found.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, such clear-cut cases existed. However, the problem lies in the fact that they do not have the relevant documents of the Republic of Croatia. In the meantime, they had a set of different documents, and what they needed to do now was to reapply for new documents of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, before we move off this topic, let me ask you, Mr. Moric: Did the availability of all these weapons impact on the crime problem that you were facing?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it did have an impact. In addition to the efforts put in by the police to collect the remaining weapons and the left-over ammunition, including the anti-armour rockets, which was heavy ordnance, there were individuals who were prone to criminal conduct and who wanted to arm themselves as soon as possible. To add to the general chaos, there were -- there was arms trafficking rife in the area. You'll understand that it was relatively easy to come by weapons at the time, and one could expect for individuals to get hold of weapons and hold on to them for a while, waiting for their price on the market to go up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us shift to another problem facing the civilian police that you referred to in the questioning to date, and that refers to looting. And I'd like to use some exhibits to take us through this and have explain some matters. And if we could bring up first 1D3049. Now, this is a criminal report that was filed 12 September 1995. If we can go to the second page, you can see that it's signed by Mr. Kardum of the crime police. And I'm interested in the entry for 31 August 1995, where it discusses the activity of a Mate Kulusic, and he was accompanied by an Alen Marin. Do you see that, sir? And reading after the name of "Alen Marin," it says --

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult, but I can make it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, let's see if we can -- if you have any difficulties, I think we can get you a hard copy. But it said this individual: "... accompanied by Alen Marin, benefitting from the inability of the unknown persons to protect their property, took several items from the abandoned house, i.e., the garage, with the intent of transporting the same to his own house in Kljuc, Drnis municipality, and thus gain illegal benefit of the property." Now, during your testimony, you were talking about looting and thievery that was just for outright gain for the individual. Now, was this the type of scenario that you were talking about? Not this specifically, but this type of scenario, was this what you were talking about when you said that?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. When I talked about the crime committed for gain, I meant theft and aggravated theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we'll offer into evidence 1D3049.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1865.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1865 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just staying with the types of people that were doing this, we just categorised those who did it for gain. And in your statement to the Prosecutor, D1842, and this is at 4893, 93 of 107, and you were talking about motivation of people to take property. You noted at line 27: "So we had people who would come back to their village and recognise their property in the neighbouring house, so they would put it -- take that, but they wouldn't take it back to their house, but would take it back to the house where they used to live, where they lived for the last three years." Going to the next page: "You had people who would -- who took other people's property, but said that they recognised that this -- that this is their property and that they recognised. So you had such a huge area which was impossible to physically control, you had such a situation." So first we were talking about looters for personal greed, and then you had information, as you discussed with the Office of the Prosecutor, people who fell into this category, that took their property that they said was theirs. Can you just elaborate on that to a degree and tell me the overall situation as it was relayed back to you, and the consequences of that.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, examples such as this one, and various versions thereof, were plentiful. As is commonly known, many or almost all non-Serbs had previously been driven out of the area; not only Croats, but others as well. In 1990 and 1991, their property was looted and homes destroyed. After the liberation of the territory, it would happen that individuals would recognise certain items as their own. However, in that event the police resorted to reasonable suspicion; was it indeed the case that the citizen had recognised any items that he stole -- his own property, or whether he was only using this as a subterfuge, as a justification. It depended on the policemen involved. It was down to his assessment and to his options to check on that. It would be highly unlikely for these individuals to actually be in possession of the bills that they had once, indeed, bought the items concerned, and there was no other way of verifying their allegations. So it was a very difficult choice or situation that the policeman manning the check-point was faced with. But it was more of a problem in legal and professional terms, rather than his own discernment of what the situation was. Most often, the police manning the check-points proceeded from the presumption of culpability, rather than the presumption of innocence, as should have been the case according to our jurisdiction. In principle, this meant that the policemen wanted, through whichever way was possible, to check whether this was, indeed, a matter of ownership or only a camouflage for theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just change the motivation of some of these people just a bit through another document, and I'd like you to examine it, because in the document there are some comments that I would like to explore with you. And that is 1D3029, a criminal report again filed on behalf of Mr. Kardum by his subordinate, dated 31 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring that up on the screen. Again, that is 1D3029.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a report to the municipal public prosecutor. If we could move to page 2 of the document, and if you can just -- actually, it's page 3 in the B/C/S, I'm being told. Thank you very much. Thank you, that's it. Just tell me, sir, when you've finished reviewing that page.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've gone through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You see that this is an aggravated theft case. It does involve an individual employed by the HV, and we'll take that at a -- I'll get into that in a little bit. But I would just like to stay with the content -- the rest of the content of this document. If we could move ahead to page 4 in the English, and 4 in the B/C/S. This is a receipt for these items. If we could turn the page in both English and B/C/S, there's another receipt. And if we could do that just one more time, there's yet another receipt. Now, if we could go on, and we have an Official Note by the crime police in the next page, page 7 in the English. And if we could go to the next Official Note concerning this individual, Mile Serdar. And I'm interested -- this is the individual who was a driver for the Croatian Army, and I'm interested in the justification that was given to the crime police for this theft. Do you see that, at the bottom of the page, there should be -- there's one last line. But the paragraph right before the last line, it said: "Given that during the occupation of Sveti Rok, they left everything behind which has now been stolen or burnt, he thought that he had every right to take now what he took, and therefore he didn't talk to anyone about this before." Now, that type of mentality and psychology, were you receiving information back from your police administrations that many of these looters were justifying their actions because they had lost all their items during the occupation from 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, in their day-to-day work the police was faced with explanations and justifications such as this one. But as you can see in this particular example at hand, this did not prevent the police from doing its police work. There was no solidarity in that sense, although you will see that there were quite a few members of the uniformed police or the crime police who had suffered the same or similar fate, or whose families had suffered the same or similar fate. With your leave, I would like to draw your attention to another relevant piece of information in the document.
