In paragraph 3, it is stated that the gentleman worked as a driver at the Logistics Base of the Croatian Army, but the relevant piece of information which would indicate the scale of the problem we were faced with was that he had been living for four years in Hotel Laguna, in a hotel room in Zagreb, which is roughly 180 kilometres away from the place where he committed this crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, just going through the rest of the document - we will go into this - if we just page through, just for the purposes of the Chamber, I don't want to say that this is the last document, there are two more Official Notes from the suspects. And if we go to page 11, it notes a referral by the state prosecutor to the Military Prosecutor's Office because Mile Serdar is employed by the Croatian Army, and also a referral to the Karlovac. One goes to the Split Military Prosecutor's Office and another one to the Karlovac Prosecutor's Office. Excuse me, then the last one is from Ivan Simic, as the military prosecutor. And we will talk about those issues in one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But at this time we would like to offer into evidence 1D3029.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1866.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1866 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You talked, Mr. Moric, about decisions that individuals at check-points have to make and what has to be done at that particular time. And the Chamber has received evidence that if a check-point -- a police at a check-point perceives that items are stolen, that he has to seize those items from the individual. Now, let me just change that circumstance just a bit through another report and ask you if this is yet another problem that causes a police officer at a check-point to have to use his own judgement. And let me bring up 1D3017. Now, this is another work order from the Benkovac -- 6th Benkovac Police Station, 13 August 1995. If I could turn to the second page and if we could look at the paragraph beginning at 1620. And this paragraph talks about the transportation of cattle, cows, calves, and sheep, loaded on in Gracac, and taking it through a check-point. And tell me after you read that last paragraph, when you have completed it, and I will talk about it a bit.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only that paragraph, or should I read through to the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you could read through the whole document. It's just one page.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this raises a problem concerning -- or an issue concerning cattle. Now, we know based on prior evidence that the civilian police would take stolen property or what they thought was stolen property from people coming through check-points, but here we have a situation of individuals that at least were suspected of transporting cattle that might have been stolen. Now, under those circumstances - and here we have cows, calves, and sheep - what is a police officer at a check-point supposed to do? And does he have the facilities at his disposal at some rural check-point to seize cows, calves, and sheep to take care of them? And the reason I ask you this question by way of background, Mr. Moric, is this: There have been items of evidence coming in from internationals where they perceived people who were transporting stolen livestock moving through check-points --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know leading questions are allowed in cross-examination, but then to explain to a witness why a question is asked, and the background, and the purpose, I think, is perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you. You may put the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll go back to my initial question. Do you remember it, Mr. Moric, or do I have to repeat it for you? And I'm talking about the problem facing an officer at a check-point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What to do with cattle, that was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep matters short. Mr. Moric, what to do with the cattle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in this example, cattle is potentially evidence. In general, in police practice at the time, police would submit evidence together with criminal reports, so as long as the investigation is being carried out, the evidence is under police care. And then upon completion of the criminal investigation, together with the criminal report and the possible suspects, the evidence is to be presented at court. Of course, in cases like this one, it is technically difficult to organise. Therefore, in cases like this one, and I must say that these colleagues of mine were lucky that in the immediate vicinity there was a farm, so that they could register that the cattle was seized and that it would be temporarily accommodated at the farm. But my colleagues in other areas, who did not have any farms in their vicinity, had serious problems with this, how to -- how to keep the evidence, how to have it fixed, and then how to physically preserve it once it has been registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how do they solve it, Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the solutions was quite unusual. Namely, we are talking about the fact that they would use an exception to what the law provides; namely, that a perpetrator or a possible perpetrator of the crime of theft would be obliged to preserve himself cattle or other evidence, which is difficult to preserve physically, until the proceedings against him are initiated. And previously the evidence would be recorded in the usual way and the receipt would be issued to this person, saying that such evidence, in this case cattle, were seized from the person who is suspected of having committed the crime, but physically would be left with the person, and the person would be legally obliged to take care of this evidence. All of that under the assumption that the person who is the suspect is interested in preserving such evidence, in particular if the person considers himself or herself not guilty and is convinced that he or she would prove innocence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, a slight intervention into the transcript. Page 52, line 2, after -- or before the word "seized," the witness mentioned another word which is, I think, quite important to be introduced into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check that. Although I find the word in a different line, but I take it that we're looking at the same. You said that, "... the evidence would be recorded in the usual way and a receipt would be issued to this person, saying that such evidence, in this case cattle, were..." and then we read, "seized from the person who is suspected of having committed a crime." Did you add anything where you said that the cattle were seized from that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that the evidence would be preserved in the usual way, and on the receipt it would be stated that in the legal sense of the word, the evidence would be seized, but physically it would be left with this person, with the obligation to take care of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand this to be that although the cattle were seized, immediately the person under whom it was seized was appointed the custodian of that seized cattle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you have understood that properly. That is right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At this time, we will offer into evidence 1D3017.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1867.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1867 is admitted into evidence. Perhaps one follow-up question. What you described as what happened with cattle, did this occasionally happen with other seized objects as well? For example, if I would have a truckload of refrigerators, not having an opportunity to store them right away, that a similar procedure would be applied; that is, that it would be recorded what was formally seized, but then the person who transported these objects or -- that it would be left in his hands and that he would be responsible for preserving those objects as evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the practice at the time was such that, with a refrigerator as an example, that wouldn't have been the case. Judging by examples of TV sets and similar, it would also not be the case. But it would be the case if someone had a great quantity of firewood, or of building materials, or similar items which, because of their volume and quantity, would simply be too big for any police facility. So if the police were to seize and preserve this as evidence, then very soon around the police station there would be a space that would seem like a public depot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My example was not about a refrigerator, but about a truckload of refrigerators, and perhaps I should say a truckload of household appliances, where the police may not have had a truck to transport them. Could a similar thing -- could a similar procedure be followed under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly it could, and there could have been a case or two like that, but I think that according to the law, an exception of this kind is envisaged only for cases that are not typical, such as when it is physically impossible to preserve such evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I just want to shift gears and talk a little bit about the authorities of the civilian police and the military police. And I'd like to show you a couple of items in evidence, starting with D1626, which is the statement of Mr. Mladen Bajic, who's now the chief state attorney for the Republic of Croatia, but during the war was a military prosecutor, and I'd like to just show you a sequence of statements or pieces of evidence and then ask you some questions. And this is all in the spirit of moving through this quickly. And if we could move to paragraph -- excuse me, point 6 or paragraph 6. It's page 3 in the English and -- paragraph 6, and there it is in the B/C/S. If you could take a quick look at that question in the first paragraph, and I'm interested in the area where Mr. Bajic says: "Thus," and this is in the second -- third sentence in the answer: "Thus the general jurisdiction was assigned to the public prosecutor, and if, in the course of a previous procedure or after the commencement of a criminal procedure, it was established that an offence falls within the scope of the work of the military justice system, the procedure would be taken over by the military prosecutor." If we can turn our attention ahead to paragraph 14, and I'm interested in the last paragraph in 14, which is page 7 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S. And it notes: "In general terms, the role of the military police in the detection and perpetrators of criminal offences is as follows: After determining that a criminal offence has been committed, the civilian police from the composition of the Ministry of the Interior conducts criminal proceedings of the case. If, in the course of processing of the case, it would be established that the perpetrator was a member of the military, the military police would then take over the criminal processing. Therefore, the minister of the interior had general jurisdiction for conducting criminal processing, and in cases where, in the course of processing, it was established that the offence was under the jurisdiction of the military justice system, criminal processing would be taken over or conducted from the beginning by the military police." I want to ask you a sequence of these, sir, just in the spirit of time, because there are several witnesses that have committed on this, and I just want to give them all to you. The next one is Judge Zoran Matulovic, who is now a judge in the County Court in Split, was a judge in the -- of the military courts, and that would be D1613. If we could bring that up on the screen. If we could turn to paragraph 9 in the English. That's on page 7 of the English. And in the B/C/S, it is page 7 in the B/C/S as well. Reading under the question -- under the question -- the paragraph 9, it notes: "When the civilian police or military police notified the duty investigating judge of the District Court (now County Court) on any incident or perpetration of a criminal offence when the perpetrator is unknown at the time, the investigation is always conducted by the investigating judge of the District Court. The investigating judge of the Military Court is autonomous. The Military Court has its own duty service, and the duty military investigating judge does not participate in the work of the Investigating Centre." Number 10. "Q. When does the investigating judge of the Military Court -" it should be have, it says having - "having territorial jurisdiction, i.e., venue, join the investigation?" We can turn the page in the English. I think we're okay in the B/C/S: "At the moment, it has been established beyond doubt that the perpetrator of the criminal offence is a soldier, i.e., when it has been established that the offence falls under the jurisdiction of the military judiciary, for instance, when military equipment has been damaged, et cetera." The point there is at the moment it has been established beyond doubt that the perpetrator is -- that the perpetrator of the criminal offence is a soldier. One last piece of evidence before we go into this, and that would be D1553, and this is the evidence -- statement by a Mr. Galovic, the county state prosecutor in Zadar. And if we could turn to the next page in both the English and the B/C/S, and I'm interested in the second question asked. "Q. Could you describe the role of the civilian police in the prevention and discovery of the perpetrators of criminal offences? "A. According to the criminal procedure law, the police take necessary actions aimed at the prevention and discovery of criminal offences, and the perpetrators in the interim, a pre-investigative procedure. "When there is reasonable suspicion that a criminal offence has been committed which is prosecuted, the police has the duty to take measures ex officio to find the perpetrator of the criminal offence, to prevent the perpetrator or the accomplice from hiding or escaping, to find and secure the traces of the criminal offence and objects that might serve as evidence, and to collect any information that might be useful to conduct a successful criminal procedure." If we could move ahead to the next page, and that would be the page -- the next page in English, and let me check on the B/C/S. And I believe that's right at the top of the page: "Q. Could you describe the role of the military police in the prevention and the discovery of perpetrators of criminal offences? "A. While performing military duties, the military police is authorised to take actions towards: Military persons serving at the Ministry of Defence and the armed forces; state officials and employees serving in the armed forces; state officials and employees of the Ministry of Defence who perform duties from the scope of the work of the Ministry of Defence and the armed forces; civilians located in military buildings that serve for defence purposes." Moving down several paragraphs in this page in the English to, "Accordingly ...," it's under the next question, same page in the B/C/S: "Accordingly, the discovery of criminal offences and perpetrators of those criminal offences was in the jurisdiction of the police, or the military police respectively, when the criminal offences fell under the jurisdiction of the military judiciary." Now, Mr. Moric, these items in evidence before the Chamber from Mr. Bajic and Judge Matulovic and Mr. Galovic concerning the law in this area, is that your understanding of how these matters were to be investigated and who had jurisdiction, either the civil element or the military element, under the various circumstances as described by these three gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, even though I'm neither an expert for criminology, nor did I manage crime police, I will try to answer as precisely as possible to your question. In general, this was how the distinction of jurisdiction was made between civilian and military police. But I would ask if we could please return on the screen the document of Mr. Bajic, because it seems to me that we should have a look at an information that is relevant in this context, if you would allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir. If we could go back to D1626, and I actually read from two entries, and I'll show them both. One is larger than the other, but we can look at both of them. In page 3 in the English, under Question 6, I read for you the -- under the answer in 6, having looked at first paragraph -- I read for you: "Thus the general jurisdiction was assigned to the public prosecutor." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. But if we could please move on to the section that talks about the jurisdiction of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, and that would be on page 7 in the English, right above paragraph 15. And again my memory is not completely accurate as to where this is in the B/C/S. Page 6 in the B/C/S. Thank you. I believe that is the other section that I read for you from Mr. Bajic, where it notes in general terms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the witness asked whether he could see a certain portion of the document. Let's first allow him to read --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am, Judge, I'm just trying to make sure that we get the right place, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, you started -- the previous section, you started reading it, whereas I think the witness is in a perfect situation to read the portion he asked for. Is this the portion, Mr. Moric, you wanted to have in front of you? Please read it and make your observations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to point out the formulation used in this sentence, which is the second in the passage beginning with the words: "In general terms ..." So the second sentence. It says here that if, in the course of the processing of the case, it would be established that the perpetrator was a member of the military, the military crime police would then take over the criminal processing. However, at the time that we are talking about, and considering the problems at the time, the situations that we were faced with most often were such that it was clear from the very beginning that these were military persons, so we didn't need the criminal processing to establish that these were military persons. And in that context, I wanted to say that in such situations, it was clear that the military police would be in charge of that from the start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With that clarification and the other items that I read to you, do you agree that that was your understanding as to how the system would work, and the processing of suspects, depending whether or not they were military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, as I'm looking at the clock. Could you find a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a suitable moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was just going to go into some other exhibits on this, but we can do that. That will take a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will have a break, and we will resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, we'd like to just develop this issue with the military police and the civilian police just a little bit more, and I'd like to direct -- just expand it past some of your comments about joint check-points, and singular check-points, and difficulties, and just to turn our attention to some work orders that are similar to what we looked at before. The first one I'd like to talk to you about is 1D3019, which is again a work order for 15 August 1995. And if we could -- if we could just take a look at that front page briefly. And when you finish, just let me know, Mr. Moric, and we can turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Turn to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you. Turn to the next page. And I'm most interested in the entry towards the middle of that page, Fitoma Jurosevic [phoen], with the seizure of the Zastava truck. It notes that the same was handed over to the military police because he was transporting a cow and 10 sheep in his trailer, on which he picked up in the village of Oklaj, and didn't have any documents for the mentioned cattle. And it notes in parenthesis "(member of the Croatian Army)." You note the first line is "handed over to the military police." And let's just look at 1D3025. This is another work order for the civilian police of the 18-19 August. Just let me know when you've glanced through that and we'll turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can turn to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Turn that page in English. If we could just read this, I'm actually interested in the paragraph beginning: "At 20.40 hours, we stopped a vehicle with license plate ZD-535-u which is operated by a member of the Croatian Army, Bozidar Mikulic, and the same vehicle, with no certificate of ownership, the same was transporting two lambs and were behaving in an unbecoming and arrogant manner towards officer, policeman; Marin, Darko. The duty service was informed of the same, and they sent the military police, who then took over the aforementioned person." If we can turn to the next one, 1D3048. This is another work order from the Knin District Police from 4-5 September 1995. If you'll glance at that page and tell me, and we'll move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Turn to the next page. I'm actually interested most specifically in the bottom portion of that page at 2110 hours. It notes: "... an army truck with registration HV-743-PF arrived at the check-point, and the same was filled with objects and the driver had a receipt which we thought was suspicious, and we requested the operative duty officer within the administration of the arrival of the military police. Upon arrival, the military police took over and removed the truck from traffic." Just moving again quickly through, 1D3050. Again, it's another work order from 20 September 1995 from the Knin Police District. If we can move to the second page. Sorry, if I could just -- thank you. If I can go back to the prior page just one moment. I note for your review point 5 in the special tasks, that: "If the person stopped and checked is an HV member, inform the military police through operative duty." If we could turn to the next page for the particular factual events, and I'm interested in the facts concerning the 1610 entry. It notes: "At 1610 we stopped a vehicle with no registration plates; make, Warburg, green in colour; with a trailer with two uniformed persons inside without military passes. And the same also didn't have a receipt for the goods they were transporting and no registration card." "The police station operative duty was notified, and the same sent a military police patrol. At 1650, Corporal Loncov," and I'm not even going to attempt the next name, "Domagoj from the 72nd Military Police Battalion took over the persons." One last entry, and this is 1D3024, and this is again from the Benkovac Police Station, 17 August 1995. And if we can turn to the next page -- is that okay to turn to the next page, Mr. Moric? Yes, so we turn to the next page, and I'm interested in entry 14, which is at 1750, describing a vehicle ZD-521-B, Zastava, 640-D, blue, Marinko Ledenko, Sonja, and Martin Ledenko, and Vuka Sava [phoen], and Sime Bobic, they were transporting two beds, a wood stove, kitchen tables, mattress. Persons and items were taken over by the Benkovac military police, due to the fact that the driver was a member of the Croatian Army 4th Brigade. Now, Mr. Moric, looking at these documents, your men in the field properly executed what they were supposed to do, i.e., if they saw something suspicious or possible of criminal activity, they were stopping these people at check-points and calling the military police so the military police could take custody of the matter; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Counsel. They did what the order told them to do. In all these documents, we were able to see on the first page, save for the last document, I believe, that the policemen specified what the specific duties were, that the vehicles had to be pulled over, and that those items in respect of which ownership could not be ascertained should be impounded. In one of the reports, mention was made of individuals transporting goods for which they had a certificate of ownership. However, the police found the certificate suspicious and asked that both the individuals and the goods concerned be taken care of, taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us -- that is probably the good example to talk about, and that would be 1D3048. If we could bring that one back on the screen, the second-to-last one, because I think that's the one that you were referring to, where your officers noted that the receipt was "suspicious."

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that could be on page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2. If we could go down to the 2110 entry towards the bottom. That's it. Now, Mr. Moric, in this scenario here we have an HV truck coming through with suspicious paperwork, that your officer thinks is suspicious. As opposed to letting this suspicious action take place or possible crime take place, he had the responsibility of keeping that individual there and then calling the military police to have them take over; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, your conclusion is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, since you've called this back --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh no -- Mr. President, please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We also see in this document, and it apparently was once attached to this document, that persons arrived in a vehicle and that they had a receipt for exporting certain items, but that the police officers were informed later on that such receipts were no longer valid. And they apparently have attached a copy of that receipt. Now, could you shed some light on what kind of receipts these were and why such receipts were not valid anymore on the 4th or the 5th of September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the case in point in this particular report, my understanding is that the individuals who were in the vehicle had some sort of a receipt indicating that the items there were owned by them, but that the police found it suspicious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I think you're looking at the wrong entry. If we can go to the entry at 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the entry at, yes, 2000 hours. Could you please read that portion of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. I have obviously misunderstood your question. This may have been one of the cases where some of the government commissioners or representatives of civilian authorities tried to issue citizens with receipts for the items that they recognised as theirs in order to be able to certify that they were, indeed, their belongings. As soon as we realised, "we" being the police, that this practice is open to abuse, we asked that the government ban the government commissioners and representatives of local authorities from resorting to such practice. We informed the police structures that they should not consider such documents as valid. I think that this is what the particular example here might be about, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would like to offer into evidence 1D3019, 1D3024, 1D3025, 1D3048, and 1D3050.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, those will become Exhibit D1868 up to and including D1872.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1868 up to and including D1872 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, we're going to shift gears just a little bit and talk about the actual planning of check-points and your discussions with General Lausic both prior to Operation Storm and after. And we know, based on the exhibits that we have seen and presented to the Chamber and you discussed, that check-points -- joint check-points were scheduled to be established, and you ordered that to your men as early as the 3rd of August, 1995. And for the record, that's P493. And we also know, in our discussions with my learned friend Mr. Kay, that you had expressed displeasure about the lack of co-operation with the military police at these check-points, and we saw that yesterday in your examination with Mr. Kay, of 10 August 1995, which would have been D46. Now, you also noted for us that as you were going through these very difficult days, you were in daily communication with Major General Lausic, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Counsel. It was necessary for us to be in frequent communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that communication obviously took the form of both oral conversations and written correspondence, as we've seen. But my question comes to your discussions with Mr. Lausic, both in person and in writing. When you were talking to him about the problems in the liberated areas and the problems that you were having with the military police, did General Lausic ever say to you that he didn't have the authority to correct those problems?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the frequent daily contacts, Mr. Lausic and I were frustrated by the state of matters in the area. However, he never said that he lacked competence, and he never referred me to any other authority for a specific or a general case, so he was the only relevant counterpart for me on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moric, you noted, in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, D1842, at e-court number 4893, line 17, that you never spoke to General Gotovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we were specifically discussing the period before, during, and after Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Moric, and my question was not as exact, and your interpretation of my question is 100 per cent correct. So if you can answer it in that context, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before, during, and after Storm, I never contacted Mr. Ante Gotovina because I didn't have any professional reasons to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moric, when you were having discussions with General Lausic about problems in the liberated areas, did he ever tell you that he needed to go back and discuss this matter with General Gotovina in order to get this matter resolved? Did he ever tell you that?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me that he would need to refer back to Mr. Gotovina on any score, and Mr. Gotovina never actually featured in my conversations with Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, shifting gears once again, I want to go back to the order that we've discussed at some length. And if I can just reference you to it, and this has to do with your order on the 18th of August of 1995, D49. If we could bring that up on the screen. Now, the item that I'd like to talk to you about is item 4, and you ordered, in item 4 -- can you turn to that? It would be the next page in English, thank you. "It should be agreed as of today an on-site investigation and forensic and operative processing will be conducted after every case of torching houses and illegal taking away of people's movable property." Now, yesterday, in your discussions with my learned friend Mr. Kay, and the President of the Chamber was asking you some questions about arson investigations, you ordered this, sir, as part of your overall plan to bring this torching of houses and looting to an end, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Given the sequence of tasks that I set out in this letter, number 4 relates to co-operation with the military police -- or, rather, number 3 relates to the co-operation with military police, and that they, too, would have to play a role in the forensic examination and criminal inquiries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's just briefly go through the results of your order, sir, and let's look at some of those results in the field. And if we could turn our attention to a sequence of documents, and we'll do this in a similar fashion as we've gone through some of the prior documents, and begin with 1D3031.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. Can we stay with this document for a moment still?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to draw your attention to item 5 in the context of what I've just said. Item 4 specifically related to co-operation with military police, that they were supposed to get involved in the process as of that date. In item 5, I allow for the possibility that should the military police be unable to carry out its duties as per item 4 -- in other words, I do want to make sure that their engagement in the process becomes greater. So we can move on. I'm sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, taking you up on that, your intention was, whether the military police was going to participate or not, you wanted your officers to make sure that an on-site investigation was done so you could bring this burning and looting to an end; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intention behind the entire document is prevention and investigation into the events that already happened, but the emphasis is on the prevention together with the military police, prevention and investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let us turn to a sequence of documents, and I'm turning to the actual fire documents or torching documents. And if we could go to 1D3031. Again, as I mentioned, Mr. Moric, in the interests of time I'd like to show you a sequence of documents. This is an Official Note from the Gracac Police Station, on 27 August 1995, concerning the reporting of an unknown person starting a fire in a house.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I point out relevant information from this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir.

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of the third paragraph, the third one from the top in this document, it is mentioned that due to detonations of ammunition heard from within the house which was torched, they couldn't come there immediately, and I believe that this tells us something about the contexts within which this kind of work had to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. If we could turn to the next document, which is 1D3032, which is on the same day, later on that day at 1710. Again, we're looking at an investigation by a duty officer sending a patrol. In the second paragraph: "Upon arrival at the site of the incident, information was obtained that an unknown perpetrator had intentionally set fire to seven family houses ..."

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document as well -- in this document, we can also see the information about the specific attitude -- the personal and professional attitude of the police officers to the incident, because it says here that they managed to extinguish one of the fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just turn to another document, again from the Gracac area, 1D3033. This is an information from the 27-28 August 1995 on reporting of two fires. If we can turn to the next page. Stay on that page in the B/C/S. It notes: "At 1755, the Knin Police Administration Duty Service was informed of the same, and after consulting with Bugojno, it was agreed to conduct an on-site investigation in the morning on 28 August 1995. The cause of the fire is unknown." If we can continue on to another matter, 1D3034. Again, we are a series of fires being reported. For instance, looking at 1550, the front page: "The fire on one of the houses was put under control; however, the remaining four houses burnt down entirely. "After consulting the operative officer, Pogarelic, it was agreed on to conduct the on-site investigation in the morning of the 31 August." And if we can turn to the next page in English. I'm not sure if that's the next page in B/C/S. It's that same page. We again see the reporting of additional fires. Now, staying with this sequence, I mean, if we just move on. After this is reported back, you mentioned during the course of your testimony with my learned friend Mr. Kay, that the crime police becomes involved. And let us just look at a sequence of those documents, beginning with 1D3035. And while I'm doing that, Mr. President, it might be best to just tender these as we move ahead, and that would be offering 1D3031 through 1D3034.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, those documents become Exhibit D1873 up to and including D1876, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1873 up to and including D1876 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just seek your guidance at this point. I know that I said two sessions. I do have a series of Crime Department reports on arson that go through here. I know that I said I'd finish by quarter of. I do have several brief areas just to cover. If I could ask the Court's leave for some short period of time on Monday, or I suppose that I could put these in through some Bar table submissions. The reason I'm interested in this, of course, Your Honour, is I pulled these yesterday because we had some discussions about arsons and times and on-site investigations, and I have a dossier of any number of investigations, so I'll be guided by how Your Honour wants to proceed. I can certainly put these in through a Bar table. Of course, we'll miss the opportunity to have this individual's comment thereon. Or I could just keep going through these and take a very short period of time on Monday. But my apologies to the Chamber about my mistaken in time claim, but I do not think, if given some additional time on Monday, that I will be running over very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest the following, Mr. Kehoe: If you would proceed now without these documents, if before Monday you try to agree with Ms. Mahindaratne on a meaningful Bar table submission of those documents that is pointing at the most relevant entries. And then if that would not have a positive result, we still can decide on Monday morning what to do. So prepare for Bar tabling, seek the assistance of Ms. Mahindaratne for that purpose, and try to finish in the next 15 minutes on the other matters you had on your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will. Thank you, Mr. President. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, we're going to move to another item, and that had to do again -- but it's yet similar. If we can go back to D49, which is your 18 order. Now, if we go to paragraph 2, this is the item that we've talked about before that talks about the operative investigations prior to the 18th of August, then you noted, in response to questions by my learned friends, that you didn't have the authority to grant immunity, but those items were going to be investigated after the area had been brought under control. And I'd like to bring an exhibit to your attention, which is a spreadsheet from the Municipal State Attorney's Office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: D568, if I can put that on the screen. D568. Now, this, of course, is in English. Do we have this in B/C/S? No? Excuse me. I do not believe -- I've been told, it's in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But nevertheless, sir, I can tell you that these are entries of crimes. And if you look at -- and this is just on the front page, having to do with the Benkovac State Attorney's Office. We can see any number of items towards the bottom of that page where crimes are committed prior to the 18th -- and if we look at column 5, prior to the 18th of August; reported, for instance, in number 20, in September of 1995, and the decision by the State Attorney's Office was in September of 1995. Now, this particular document is replete with those examples of burning and looting charges being filed for events that took place prior to the 18th of August, 1995. Now, again, was it your understanding, as you moved through, that those items would continue to be processed once the area was brought under control?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just -- the 27th, I think Mr. Kehoe mentioned the date 27th of September. It's not reported, the date of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no. If I may. If we can go through the left-hand column and go down to, say, the 20th entry, the Benkovac police station, it notes in column 5: "Date and criminal offence was committed, August 5th, 1995. Date it was reported, 15th of September, 1995. Decision by the State Prosecutor's Office, 27 September 1995," with the Court decision in 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that this resolves your problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Moric, going back to my question, was that your understanding, that these matters would continue to be pursued after your preventive measures had taken hold?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, that was the idea, that was the intention, that we should focus on prevention. And as for what had already happened, we would clarify that once we checked the spate of negative events, as I described it. And this is what actually did happen, in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you say "in practice." Is that -- based on your knowledge as the assistant minister, was that how the police administrations, to your knowledge, interpreted your order of the 18th of August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is not a single document, and no one from police administrations asked what this was about. And if they believed that this was incorrect, professionally or legally, they were duty-bound to warn me that I was requesting something that was not professionally or legally proper. So it was clear, from our daily communication, what this was all about and what the intentions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me go through the last subject on this score, and not on this issue but just generally what I would like to talk to you about, Mr. Moric, with the caveat that we may address some issue on Monday morning. But I would like to address to you certain allegations made by the Prosecution that involves the civilian police, and it involves the crimes that you have talked about over the past several days. And I'd like to read to you some of the statements being made by the Office of the Prosecutor in their pre-trial brief. And I would, for the purposes of this, focus the Prosecution and my learned friends on paragraph 51 and the allegations concerning the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think it is proper to read to a witness off the pre-trial brief. Mr. Kehoe could just ask the questions on a factual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm putting the Prosecution's case to the witness. This is the Prosecution's case concerning the participation of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that putting the Prosecution's case or putting evidential material is not the same, Mr. Kehoe. Even if in a pre-trial brief you refer to some evidential material, witnesses are expected to testify on the basis of the questions put to them and not, at least not in first instance, comment on what other evidential material may bring.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will be guided by what Your Honour would like me to do. My only point with this is there are specific allegations made by the Prosecution concerning the participation of the civilian police in the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let's avoid that one witness starts commenting, at least to start with. I'm not saying that under no circumstances you could put to a witness what someone else has said, but let's first hear the testimony of that witness not in the form of a comment on what other evidence may bring us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. And I will not read this for Your Honour's clarification. We can move on. I was going to refer to paragraph 51 of the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief as well as paragraph 29 of the indictment. So I won't read those. I will move on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But I need to ask you this question, Mr. Moric: Based on your experience and your years in the Ministry of the Interior, both in Zagreb and in the field, did you ever participate, or do you know anybody that participated in some agreement to allow actions to take place and allow crimes to take place in order to ensure: one, that the Serb population was driven out of the Krajina and, two, to ensure that they never returned? Did you ever know of anyone participating in that in the Ministry of the Interior or anywhere else; did you?

utterances.speaker: Josko Moric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I never heard nor felt an atmosphere in the Ministry of the Interior which would go in that direction. No one who was discharging any duty within the Ministry of the Interior at the time thought that in any context whatsoever the development and the number of crimes were not something bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I have no further questions of you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. I think, Ms. Mahindaratne, it doesn't make much sense to invite you to start your cross-examination. We'd rather leave that until Monday. Could I already invite Madam Usher to escort Mr. Moric out of the courtroom. Mr. Moric, I instruct you again in the same way as I did the previous days; that is, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether already given or whether still to be given. And we would like to see you back on Monday, 9.00 in the morning, in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before adjourning, the Chamber would like to express its appreciation for the work that Mr. Monkhouse has done for us for quite a long time. His accuracy, his energy, and his commitment will for the future to be benefit of Chambers, although not this Chamber, from what I understand. Initially, I thought that I would say I would speak on behalf of all of you, but I know that there are various instructions. In an orchestra, the violin players would tick their bows on their orchestra lecterns. In school rooms, often the knuckles are used by ticking them on the tables to express the joining in the praise. Even, I think, in the House of Commons they use yelling now and then as a tradition to express that one joins in what has been said. I all give you 30 seconds to express, in your own way, that you join. And for those who have not brought their violin bows, we could try to find some, but I give you 30 seconds to express that, and we'll then adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, I think I haven't been elected, but I'll take the floor here on behalf of us all to agree with what Your Honour has said. We do have a memento for Mr. Registrar. I will say that it hasn't been looted, and I don't know how to jump-start it. We're all wearing black because Mr. Registrar is leaving us, but one moment and I'll pull it out here. We have a microphone here for Mr. Registrar. We know you're going to miss the microphone, so we just thought we'd give you an old one for a keepsake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it from the hand-clapping that everyone joins in the expression of appreciation, and of course the Chamber is very happy to have Mr. Monkhouse among their ranks. We adjourn. Accurately, guided by the little yellow note given to me by Mr. Monkhouse, we'll adjourn until Monday, the 7th of December, 9.00, Courtroom I, which will not be the same as it is today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
